question: What are Redis data structures and when do you use each in Python applications?
title: Redis Data Structures for Python
direct_answer: String: simple key-value, counters, session tokens. List: ordered queue, recent activity feed (LPUSH/LTRIM). Hash: object-like storage, user profiles. Set: unique members, online users, tags. Sorted Set: leaderboards, rate limiting with scores as timestamps. HyperLogLog: approximate count of unique values. All operations are O(1) or O(log n) — Redis is single-threaded so all are atomic.
interviewer_intent: Tests Redis depth beyond 'it's a cache'. Knowing the right data structure for the problem is the mark of Redis fluency.

sections.title: Redis data structure guide
sections.content:
Redis is not just a key-value store — it has five main data structures plus specialized types.

String: GET/SET/INCR/DECR. Atomic increment (INCR counter:users) is useful for rate limiting and feature flags. SETEX sets with TTL in one command.

List: LPUSH (left push), RPOP (right pop) for queue. LPUSH + LTRIM maintains a fixed-size recent-events buffer. BRPOP blocks until an item is available — simple task queue.

Hash: HSET/HGET/HMGET for field-level access. Store user profiles without serializing the entire object. HINCRBY for per-field counters.

Set: SADD/SISMEMBER (O(1)). SUNION/SINTER/SDIFF for set operations. Use for 'users who liked this post', tag systems, online presence.

Sorted Set: ZADD(key, score, member)/ZRANGE. Score is a float for ordering. Use for: leaderboards (score = points), rate limiting sliding window (score = timestamp), expiring members.

sections.title: Redis data structure patterns
sections.content:
import redis.asyncio as aioredis

r = aioredis.from_url('redis://localhost')

# String: counter
await r.incr('page:views:article:123')  # atomic increment
await r.setex('session:abc123', 3600, user_id)  # TTL

# List: recent activity feed (fixed size)
await r.lpush('activity:user:1', event_json)
await r.ltrim('activity:user:1', 0, 99)  # keep last 100
recent = await r.lrange('activity:user:1', 0, 9)  # get last 10

# Hash: user profile
await r.hset('user:1', mapping={'name': 'Alice', 'email': 'alice@ex.com'})
name = await r.hget('user:1', 'name')
await r.hincrby('user:1', 'login_count', 1)  # increment one field

# Set: online users
await r.sadd('online:users', user_id)
await r.srem('online:users', user_id)  # on disconnect
count = await r.scard('online:users')  # count
is_online = await r.sismember('online:users', user_id)  # O(1)

# Sorted Set: leaderboard
await r.zadd('leaderboard:game:1', {user_id: score})
top_10 = await r.zrevrange('leaderboard:game:1', 0, 9, withscores=True)
rank = await r.zrevrank('leaderboard:game:1', user_id)

# Sorted Set: sliding window rate limit
import time
now = time.time()
window = 60  # seconds
pipe = r.pipeline()
pipe.zremrangebyscore(f'ratelimit:{user_id}', 0, now - window)
pipe.zadd(f'ratelimit:{user_id}', {now: now})
pipe.zcard(f'ratelimit:{user_id}')
pipe.expire(f'ratelimit:{user_id}', window)
_, _, count, _ = await pipe.execute()

seo.metaTitle: Redis Data Structures for Python — String, List, Hash, Set, Sorted Set
seo.metaDescription: Redis data structures in Python: String counters, List queues, Hash profiles, Set membership, Sorted Set leaderboards and sliding window rate limiting.

speakable_v2.hook: Redis isn't just a cache — the data structure you choose determines what operations are available and what problems become trivial.

beats.content: String for simple values and counters. INCR is atomic — no race condition for view counters or feature flag toggles. SETEX sets and expires in one command.

Sorted Set is underused. Every member has a score for ordering. Leaderboards: score = points. Sliding window rate limit: score = timestamp, ZREMRANGEBYSCORE removes old entries. Time complexity is O(log n) for insertions.
redis.pipeline() batches commands — send them all in one round trip. Critical for latency-sensitive operations that touch Redis multiple times.

speakable_v2.cap: Redis is single-threaded — all commands are serialized. That's why INCR is atomic and you can implement rate limiters without external locks.
speakable_v2.followup_handoff: Follow up with Redis pub/sub for real-time notifications, or Lua scripts for atomic multi-step operations.
